answer.exemplar: Two planes are parallel when they lie in different planes and share a direction, which is the same idea as two parallel lines in a flat figure, and the consequence is that a single direction meets both of them squarely. Take a line that meets the first plane at right angles. Translate it along itself until it reaches the second plane, and because the two planes share a direction, the translated line still meets the second at right angles. Every other line perpendicular to the first can be moved the same way, and each arrives at the second still perpendicular, so all such lines point the same way. That shared direction is the common normal, and it is unique to the pair of parallel planes: it is perpendicular to both, so nothing else can be, and the distance between the planes is measured along it. This gives a useful test, since a solid's height is the perpendicular distance between its two parallel bases, and any measurement taken obliquely between them is longer than the height and has to be resolved before it can be used. A line running parallel to the planes is a different notion entirely, since it never meets them at all.

questions.explanation: The translation argument is what makes the answer solid, since a line carried along its own direction into the second plane must still cross it squarely if the two share a direction. The answer should then name the common normal as unique to the pair, and connect it to the standard use, which is measuring the height of a solid as the perpendicular distance between its parallel bases. Saying that a line perpendicular to one is automatically perpendicular to the other without the translation step leaves a real gap in the reasoning.
questions.hint: Take a line perpendicular to one plane and move it along its own direction into the other.

answer.exemplar: A prism on a given base and a pyramid on that same base with the same perpendicular height hold their volumes in the ratio of 3 to 1, and the reason is what happens to the cross-sections as the distance from the base grows. Cut both solids by a plane parallel to the base at height y. The prism's cross-section is its full base, of area B, at every height, so its volume is B times h. The pyramid's cross-section at height y is a similar figure scaled by y over h, since everything above that plane is a smaller pyramid, so its area is B times the square of y over h. Integrating that from the base to the apex gives B times h over 3, and the ratio of the two volumes is therefore 3 to 1, with the pyramid holding exactly one third of the matching prism. The same figure appears from the net, since a pyramid's faces are triangles whose areas are one half of base times slant height, and those triangular faces total one half of the total area of the corresponding prism's faces. The ratio matters because it converts between the two shapes without recomputing anything, so a pyramid's volume can be found from a prism's on the same base and height, and a composite solid's pieces can be checked against each other. It is also why the height must be the perpendicular one, since any other measurement would change the prism the pyramid is being compared against.

questions.explanation: The cross-section argument is the heart of the answer, because it shows that the pyramid's slices shrink by the square of the height fraction, and integrating that is what produces the third. The net argument is a useful second route and much easier to state, and giving both is what makes the ratio convincing rather than quoted. The closing point about the perpendicular height belongs here too, since a slanted measurement would silently compare against a different prism.
questions.hint: Compare what a slice parallel to the base looks like in each solid, and use a net as a second route.

answer.exemplar: A cross-section is the flat face a cutting plane leaves behind, and its boundary is made of exactly the points where that plane meets the solid's surface, so the plane alone decides the shape. A plane that passes through all four vertical edges' midpoints of a cube meets four of its faces, one edge in each, and each side of the section lies in a single face, with opposite sides lying in opposite faces. Those pairs are parallel, so the section is a parallelogram, and for the mid-edge cut the side lengths are an edge of the cube and a face diagonal, which makes it a rectangle and not a square. Tilting the same cube's plane a little changes both the shape and the size, and tilting it far enough produces a triangle or a hexagon, which is why a set of sections is the standard way to identify an unfamiliar solid. Two things a section cannot tell you are worth stating. It is not a view, because nothing is removed and the interior stays hidden, so a projection from above is a different picture with a different purpose. And it is not the same thing as the solid's own measurements, since its volume and total surface fix no particular section, although the volume does bound how large any section can be. The section records the geometry the plane encountered and nothing more.

questions.explanation: The answer should give the general principle first, that the section's boundary is the set of points where the plane meets the surface, and then apply it to the cube, naming the four faces met and concluding rectangle rather than square with the two side lengths identified. Distinguishing a section from a view is a necessary part of the answer, and so is noting that different tilts give different shapes, since that is the reason sections are used to identify solids.
questions.hint: Start from what forms the boundary of a section, then apply it to the named cube cut.

answer.exemplar: A scale factor stretches a figure in every direction at once, and the number of directions a quantity measures is what decides how the factor lands on it. A length measures the extent in one direction, so multiplying each length by k multiplies the length by k. An area measures the product of two perpendicular extents, and the factor is applied independently to each of them, so the area is multiplied by k times k, which is k squared. A volume measures the product of three extents, so it is multiplied by k cubed. The squaring is not a special fact about area, it is arithmetic: an area is a product, and a product of two scaled factors is their product. A worked check is enough to fix the idea, since doubling both sides of a square multiplies its area by 4, and tripling both sides multiplies it by 9. This is exactly why a scale model is misleading if only the heights are compared, since halving a building's height halves its apparent proportions while its footprint shrinks by four and its volume by eight. The same reasoning converts a real figure to a model, and it runs in reverse to go from a model back, so a model at 1 to 50 that is 48 centimetres tall stands for a building 2400 centimetres, which is 24 metres, high.

questions.explanation: The answer should build the whole thing on the observation that area and volume are products, so the factor simply multiplies, and that is the reason rather than a rule to be memorised. A concrete doubling or tripling check makes it stick, and the consequence about scale models is what gives the idea its point, since heights halve while areas quarter and volumes eighth. The reverse direction, model to reality, is worth one line since that is the direction most calculations actually run.
questions.hint: Count how many independent directions each quantity measures, and treat area and volume as products.
